The Chain of Responsibility Pattern Solves a Routing and Decision Flow Problem Many systems process requests through a sequence of checks and transformations:
authentication authorization validation enrichment execution The anti-pattern is one large method that does all of this with nested branching. It becomes fragile, hard to test, and difficult to evolve when steps change.
The Chain of Responsibility pattern solves this by passing a request through a chain of handlers. Each handler can process the request, pass it onward, or stop the chain.
In Java systems, this is a practical pattern for request pipelines, middleware-style processing, and policy enforcement flows.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Chain of Responsibility as:
Avoid coupling the sender of a request to its receiver by giving more than one object a chance to handle the request.
Practically, this means:
define a common handler contract link handlers in sequence let each handler decide whether and how to continue This keeps request senders decoupled from concrete handling logic and order details.
Why Teams Use Chain of Responsibility Without this pattern, teams usually get:
giant conditional dispatch blocks duplicate pre-check logic in multiple services difficult-to-reuse validation/enforcement steps brittle control flow when adding/removing stages With a chain:
each concern becomes a focused handler ordering is explicit and configurable tests can target each stage independently cross-cutting pipeline behavior becomes composable Java Example: API Request Processing Pipeline Request and response public record ApiRequest(String userId, String token, String payload) {} public record ApiResponse(int statusCode, String body) {} Handler contract public interface RequestHandler { ApiResponse handle(ApiRequest request); } Base chain helper public abstract class AbstractHandler implements RequestHandler { private RequestHandler next; public AbstractHandler setNext(RequestHandler next) { this.next = next; return this; } protected ApiResponse next(ApiRequest request) { if (next == null) { return new ApiResponse(200, "OK"); } return next.handle(request); } } Concrete handlers public class AuthenticationHandler extends AbstractHandler { @Override public ApiResponse handle(ApiRequest request) { if (request.token() == null || request.token().isBlank()) { return new ApiResponse(401, "Missing auth token"); } return next(request); } } public class AuthorizationHandler extends AbstractHandler { @Override public ApiResponse handle(ApiRequest request) { if (!request.userId().startsWith("user-")) { return new ApiResponse(403, "User is not authorized"); } return next(request); } } public class ValidationHandler extends AbstractHandler { @Override public ApiResponse handle(ApiRequest request) { if (request.payload() == null || request.payload().isBlank()) { return new ApiResponse(400, "Payload cannot be empty"); } return next(request); } } public class BusinessHandler extends AbstractHandler { @Override public ApiResponse handle(ApiRequest request) { return new ApiResponse(200, "Processed request for " + request.userId()); } } Chain composition AuthenticationHandler authn = new AuthenticationHandler(); AuthorizationHandler authz = new AuthorizationHandler(); ValidationHandler validation = new ValidationHandler(); BusinessHandler business = new BusinessHandler(); authn.setNext(authz).setNext(validation).setNext(business); ApiResponse response = authn.handle(new ApiRequest("user-123", "token-abc", "hello")); System.out.println(response.statusCode() + " - " + response.body()); This gives clear, composable request handling with short-circuit behavior.
Another Java Example: Expense Approval Chain This pattern is common in approval workflows.
Request public record ExpenseRequest(String requesterId, long amountCents) {} Handler public interface ExpenseApprover { boolean approve(ExpenseRequest request); } Approvers public class TeamLeadApprover implements ExpenseApprover { private ExpenseApprover next; public TeamLeadApprover setNext(ExpenseApprover next) { this.next = next; return this; } @Override public boolean approve(ExpenseRequest request) { if (request.amountCents() <= 50_000) { return true; } return next != null && next.approve(request); } } public class DirectorApprover implements ExpenseApprover { private ExpenseApprover next; public DirectorApprover setNext(ExpenseApprover next) { this.next = next; return this; } @Override public boolean approve(ExpenseRequest request) { if (request.amountCents() <= 500_000) { return true; } return next != null && next.approve(request); } } public class CfoApprover implements ExpenseApprover { @Override public boolean approve(ExpenseRequest request) { return request.amountCents() <= 5_000_000; } } This keeps escalation logic clean and extensible.
Chain of Responsibility vs Command Chain of Responsibility routes a request through multiple potential handlers. Command encapsulates a request as an object for execution, queueing, or undo. They can be combined (commands flowing through a chain), but they solve different problems.
Chain of Responsibility vs Decorator Chain of Responsibility: each handler may stop or continue request flow. Decorator: always wraps/delegates while adding behavior around the same operation. If early termination and conditional handling are core requirements, Chain is usually the better fit.
SOLID Alignment This pattern aligns strongly with SOLID:
Single Responsibility Principle Each handler owns one concern.
Open/Closed Principle Add or reorder handlers without modifying existing handler internals.
Dependency Inversion Principle Pipeline assembly depends on handler abstractions, not concrete end-to-end logic blocks.
This makes request-processing architectures easier to evolve safely.
Common Mistakes 1. Hidden chain ordering Order changes behavior. Chain composition should be explicit and test-covered.
2. Handlers doing too much Overgrown handlers become mini-monoliths. Keep stages narrow and focused.
3. Unclear stop/continue semantics Document and enforce whether handlers should short-circuit on failure or always continue.
4. Missing observability Without logging/metrics per stage, production debugging is painful.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Chain of Responsibility when:
request handling is multi-stage and likely to evolve each stage has distinct concerns early exits and conditional routing are meaningful Avoid it when:
processing is simple and linear with little variation handler abstraction adds indirection without clear benefits a direct service flow is easier to understand and maintain Pattern value comes from clear stage boundaries, not from introducing pipelines by default.
Final Thoughts The Chain of Responsibility pattern is a practical way to turn complex request processing into modular, composable stages.
In Java, it works especially well for middleware-like flows, policy pipelines, and approval chains where concerns need to remain isolated yet ordered.
Used well, it improves maintainability and extensibility. Used carelessly, it creates opaque request paths and debugging pain.
The practical standard is clear:
keep handlers focused make ordering explicit define stop/continue rules clearly instrument each stage for visibility That is how you build request pipelines that scale with system complexity instead of collapsing under it.

The Command Pattern Solves a Request Management Problem In many systems, actions are not just method calls. They are business requests with lifecycle needs:
execute now or later queue and retry audit who requested what support undo/redo replay during recovery When request logic is embedded directly in UI handlers, controllers, or services, these capabilities become difficult to add consistently.
The Command pattern solves this by encapsulating a request as an object. The request object carries execution behavior (and optionally undo behavior), allowing requests to be queued, logged, composed, retried, and replayed in a structured way.
In Java systems, this is one of the most practical behavioral patterns for workflow orchestration and operational control.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Command as:
Encapsulate a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with queues, requests, and operations.
In practical terms:
define a command interface represent each action as a concrete command class invokers trigger command execution receivers hold business behavior implementation This separates “what to do” from “when/how it is invoked.”
Why Teams Use Command Without Command, systems often accumulate:
controller methods packed with business action details duplicated retry/audit logic around each endpoint brittle switch-based dispatchers poor traceability for operational actions With Command:
actions become explicit units dispatch and execution can evolve independently command metadata can be logged uniformly queues/schedulers can process commands consistently This is especially valuable in admin tooling, workflow engines, and task execution systems.
Java Example: Basic Command Structure Command contract public interface Command { void execute(); } Receiver public class AccountService { public void freeze(String accountId) { System.out.println("Freezing account " + accountId); } public void unfreeze(String accountId) { System.out.println("Unfreezing account " + accountId); } } Concrete command public class FreezeAccountCommand implements Command { private final AccountService accountService; private final String accountId; public FreezeAccountCommand(AccountService accountService, String accountId) { this.accountService = accountService; this.accountId = accountId; } @Override public void execute() { accountService.freeze(accountId); } } Invoker public class CommandBus { public void dispatch(Command command) { command.execute(); } } Usage AccountService accountService = new AccountService(); Command command = new FreezeAccountCommand(accountService, "acct-123"); new CommandBus().dispatch(command); This decouples request creation from execution orchestration.
Java Example: Command with Undo Undo support is one of the classic strengths of this pattern.
Undoable command contract public interface UndoableCommand { void execute(); void undo(); } Concrete command public class FreezeAccountUndoableCommand implements UndoableCommand { private final AccountService accountService; private final String accountId; private boolean executed; public FreezeAccountUndoableCommand(AccountService accountService, String accountId) { this.accountService = accountService; this.accountId = accountId; } @Override public void execute() { accountService.freeze(accountId); executed = true; } @Override public void undo() { if (!executed) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot undo before execution"); } accountService.unfreeze(accountId); } } Invoker with history import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; public class UndoableCommandBus { private final Deque<UndoableCommand> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); public void dispatch(UndoableCommand command) { command.execute(); history.push(command); } public void undoLast() { UndoableCommand command = history.poll(); if (command == null) { throw new IllegalStateException("No command to undo"); } command.undo(); } } This gives structured undo semantics without exposing receiver internals to callers.
Java Example: Queued Command Processing Command objects are natural queue payloads.
import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.LinkedBlockingQueue; public class QueuedCommandProcessor { private final BlockingQueue<Command> queue = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(); public void submit(Command command) { queue.add(command); } public void processNext() throws InterruptedException { Command command = queue.take(); command.execute(); } } This separates producer timing from execution timing, which is often essential in operational systems.
Command vs Strategy These patterns are related but different:
Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms. Command encapsulates invocable requests/actions. If your problem is “which algorithm should run,” think Strategy.
If your problem is “how to represent, queue, execute, track, or undo an action,” think Command.
Command vs Chain of Responsibility Command wraps one request as an object. Chain of Responsibility routes a request through multiple handlers until one handles it. They can be combined, but they solve different concerns.
SOLID Alignment Command strongly supports SOLID principles:
Single Responsibility Principle Each command class owns one action.
Open/Closed Principle Add new actions by adding new command types, not by editing central dispatch conditionals.
Dependency Inversion Principle Invokers depend on command interfaces, not concrete business services.
This promotes modular action design and easier extension over time.
Common Mistakes 1. Putting too much logic in invokers Invokers should orchestrate execution, not absorb command business rules.
2. Weak command identity and metadata In production systems, commands usually need IDs, timestamps, actor context, and correlation IDs for observability.
3. Non-idempotent retries without safeguards Queued or retried commands must consider duplicate execution risks.
4. Overusing command classes for trivial one-off calls If an action is simple and has no scheduling/audit/undo needs, a direct call may be cleaner.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Command when:
actions need to be queued, audited, retried, or undone request handling must be decoupled from request invocation action catalogs are growing and need structured dispatch Avoid Command when:
direct method calls are sufficient and stable introducing command classes adds ceremony without operational value there is no realistic need for deferred execution, history, or replay Pattern discipline means matching abstraction to workflow and operational requirements.
Final Thoughts The Command pattern is valuable because modern systems often need to treat actions as durable, observable, and schedulable units, not just immediate method calls.
In Java, Command gives teams a clean way to model actions for queueing, undo, replay, and orchestration while keeping invokers decoupled from business receivers.
Used well, it improves extensibility and operational control. Used carelessly, it creates class sprawl without meaningful benefit.
The practical standard is clear:
model meaningful actions as commands keep receiver logic cohesive keep invokers lean design for retries, idempotency, and observability where commands are durable That is how you turn request handling into a maintainable system capability instead of scattered control flow.

The Iterator Pattern Solves a Traversal Encapsulation Problem Collections are everywhere in software systems, but traversal logic should not leak data structure internals.
Without a clear iteration contract, client code often becomes tightly coupled to:
index-based loops tied to list implementations tree traversal details embedded in services ad hoc pagination logic repeated in multiple classes The Iterator pattern solves this by providing a standard way to access elements sequentially without exposing the underlying representation.
In Java, this is both foundational and practical. The standard Iterator interface is a direct embodiment of this pattern, and custom iterators remain useful for domain-specific traversal behaviors.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Iterator as:
Provide a way to access the elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation.
In practical terms:
aggregate owns storage details iterator owns traversal behavior client consumes a stable traversal interface This keeps data structures replaceable and client logic cleaner.
Why Teams Use Iterator in Real Systems Without iterator abstractions, callers often assume too much about collection layout.
That causes:
brittle client code when internal structures change duplicated traversal logic inconsistent filtering/ordering behavior With iterator-based APIs:
traversal behavior is centralized clients depend on sequence contract, not storage mechanics internal representation can evolve safely This is especially useful for custom aggregates, streamed data access, and pagination abstractions.
Java Example: Custom Iterator for a Backlog Aggregate Domain model public record BacklogItem(String id, String title, int priority) {} Aggregate import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; public class Backlog implements Iterable<BacklogItem> { private final List<BacklogItem> items = new ArrayList<>(); public void add(BacklogItem item) { items.add(item); } @Override public Iterator<BacklogItem> iterator() { return new PriorityAscendingIterator(items); } } Custom iterator import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Comparator; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.List; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; public class PriorityAscendingIterator implements Iterator<BacklogItem> { private final List<BacklogItem> sorted; private int index = 0; public PriorityAscendingIterator(List<BacklogItem> source) { this.sorted = new ArrayList<>(source); this.sorted.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(BacklogItem::priority)); } @Override public boolean hasNext() { return index < sorted.size(); } @Override public BacklogItem next() { if (!hasNext()) { throw new NoSuchElementException("No more backlog items"); } return sorted.get(index++); } } Usage Backlog backlog = new Backlog(); backlog.add(new BacklogItem("B-102", "Refactor checkout", 3)); backlog.add(new BacklogItem("B-101", "Fix payment timeout", 1)); backlog.add(new BacklogItem("B-103", "Improve logging", 2)); for (BacklogItem item : backlog) { System.out.println(item.id() + " -> priority " + item.priority()); } Clients get ordered traversal without needing to know how ordering is implemented.
Another Java Example: Tree Iterator Iterators are especially useful for hierarchical structures.
Component import java.util.List; public interface OrgNode { String name(); List<OrgNode> children(); } Iterator with depth-first traversal import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; import java.util.Iterator; import java.util.NoSuchElementException; public class DepthFirstOrgIterator implements Iterator<OrgNode> { private final Deque<OrgNode> stack = new ArrayDeque<>(); public DepthFirstOrgIterator(OrgNode root) { stack.push(root); } @Override public boolean hasNext() { return !stack.isEmpty(); } @Override public OrgNode next() { if (!hasNext()) { throw new NoSuchElementException("No more nodes"); } OrgNode current = stack.pop(); var children = current.children(); for (int i = children.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--) { stack.push(children.get(i)); } return current; } } This keeps traversal behavior reusable and separate from node storage details.
External Iterator vs Internal Iterator Two common styles:
External iterator: client controls iteration (hasNext()/next()). Internal iterator: aggregate controls iteration and invokes callback/lambda. Java’s Iterator is external, while forEach-style APIs are internal.
Use external iteration when caller needs flow control (break, resume, conditional advancement).
Use internal iteration when declarative processing is clearer.
Iterator and Fail-Fast Behavior in Java Many Java collection iterators are fail-fast: if the collection is structurally modified during iteration (outside iterator methods), a ConcurrentModificationException may occur.
This is a safety feature, not a synchronization guarantee.
For concurrent mutation scenarios, use appropriate concurrent collections or snapshot iterators when semantics require stable traversal views.
Iterator vs Stream In modern Java:
Iterator is imperative and stateful traversal. Stream is declarative pipeline processing. Streams are often preferable for transformation pipelines; iterators are useful when you need custom traversal control, lazy stepping, or backward-compatible APIs.
Both can coexist cleanly in mature codebases.
SOLID Alignment Iterator aligns with SOLID principles:
Single Responsibility Principle Aggregates manage data; iterators manage traversal mechanics.
Open/Closed Principle You can add new traversal strategies (e.g., priority, depth-first, breadth-first) without modifying aggregate clients.
Dependency Inversion Principle Clients depend on Iterator/Iterable abstractions instead of concrete data structure internals.
This supports maintainable evolution of collection-heavy domains.
Common Mistakes 1. Exposing mutable internals through iteration If iterator returns mutable internal references without boundaries, encapsulation is weakened.
2. Mixing traversal side effects into next() Keep iteration mechanics predictable. Side effects should be explicit and testable.
3. Ignoring end-of-sequence contracts next() must throw NoSuchElementException when exhausted.
4. Implementing unnecessary custom iterators Prefer built-in collections and streams unless custom traversal semantics are truly needed.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Iterator when:
clients need uniform sequential access traversal logic is non-trivial or reusable internal representation should remain hidden Avoid custom Iterator when:
built-in collection iteration is already enough added abstraction does not provide clear traversal value stream pipelines express the behavior more clearly Pattern discipline means introducing custom iterators for real traversal concerns, not for stylistic consistency.
Final Thoughts The Iterator pattern is foundational because traversal is universal, but representation should remain encapsulated.
In Java, it underpins the collections ecosystem and remains valuable for domain-specific traversal strategies where simple loops are not sufficient.
Used well, Iterator keeps client code decoupled from storage details and makes traversal behavior reusable and testable. Used carelessly, it can add unnecessary complexity or leak internals.
The practical standard is clear:
separate traversal from storage define predictable iterator contracts choose built-in iteration first, custom iterators when justified test traversal edge cases (empty, single, deep, concurrent mutation semantics) That is how you keep collection-heavy code understandable and resilient as models evolve.

Without a clear iteration contract, client code often becomes tightly coupled to:

  • index-based loops tied to list implementations
  • tree traversal details embedded in services
  • ad hoc pagination logic repeated in multiple classes

The Iterator pattern solves this by providing a standard way to access elements sequentially without exposing the underlying representation.

The Observer Pattern Solves a Change Propagation Problem In most systems, important events trigger follow-up work:
an order is created, then inventory is reserved a payment succeeds, then receipts are sent a user registers, then analytics and onboarding flows run The anti-pattern is coupling all of those actions directly into one service. That creates rigid orchestration, fragile dependencies, and high regression risk whenever subscribers change.
The Observer pattern solves this by defining a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all dependents are notified automatically.
In Java systems, this is a practical foundation for event-driven design at both in-process and distributed boundaries.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Observer as:
Define a one-to-many dependency between objects so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified and updated automatically.
Practically, this means:
a subject/publisher emits changes one or more observers/subscribers react publisher and subscribers remain loosely coupled through interfaces This allows subscriber behavior to evolve without rewriting publisher logic.
Why Teams Use Observer Without Observer, teams usually end up with:
deeply coupled service calls repetitive notification code in business services hard-coded dependency chains frequent regressions when adding/removing side effects With Observer:
event producers focus on core state changes consumers subscribe independently side effects can be added with minimal impact on producers This pattern is especially useful where business events fan out to multiple independent concerns.
Java Example: In-Process Order Event Notifications Event model public record OrderCreatedEvent(String orderId, String userId, long amountCents) {} Observer contract public interface OrderCreatedObserver { void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event); } Subject/publisher import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; public class OrderEventPublisher { private final List<OrderCreatedObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); public void subscribe(OrderCreatedObserver observer) { observers.add(observer); } public void unsubscribe(OrderCreatedObserver observer) { observers.remove(observer); } public void publish(OrderCreatedEvent event) { for (OrderCreatedObserver observer : observers) { observer.onOrderCreated(event); } } } Concrete observers public class InventoryReservationObserver implements OrderCreatedObserver { @Override public void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event) { System.out.println("Reserving inventory for order " + event.orderId()); } } public class ReceiptEmailObserver implements OrderCreatedObserver { @Override public void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event) { System.out.println("Sending receipt to user " + event.userId()); } } public class AnalyticsObserver implements OrderCreatedObserver { @Override public void onOrderCreated(OrderCreatedEvent event) { System.out.println("Tracking analytics for order " + event.orderId()); } } Producer usage public class OrderService { private final OrderEventPublisher publisher; public OrderService(OrderEventPublisher publisher) { this.publisher = publisher; } public void createOrder(String orderId, String userId, long amountCents) { // core order persistence logic publisher.publish(new OrderCreatedEvent(orderId, userId, amountCents)); } } The order service publishes one event; subscribers evolve independently.
Synchronous vs Asynchronous Notification Observer can be implemented synchronously or asynchronously.
Synchronous (in-process, direct call) simple and predictable easier transactional reasoning subscriber failures can affect publisher flow Asynchronous (queue/event bus) better decoupling and resilience improved throughput for slow subscribers requires delivery semantics, retries, and idempotency design For local domain events inside one process, synchronous Observer is often enough.
For cross-service integration and high fan-out, asynchronous eventing is usually the better architecture.
Java Example: Asynchronous Observer Style with Executor import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; public class AsyncOrderEventPublisher { private final List<OrderCreatedObserver> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4); public void subscribe(OrderCreatedObserver observer) { observers.add(observer); } public void publish(OrderCreatedEvent event) { for (OrderCreatedObserver observer : observers) { executor.submit(() -> observer.onOrderCreated(event)); } } } This shifts observer execution off the main thread, but also introduces concurrency and error-handling requirements.
Observer vs Pub/Sub These terms are related but not identical:
Observer is usually an in-process object pattern. Publish/Subscribe often refers to distributed messaging through brokers. Observer is often the conceptual starting point for event-driven architecture, while pub/sub is the distributed systems implementation style.
Observer vs Mediator Observer: one publisher notifies many subscribers. Mediator: central coordinator manages interactions among peers. If your main need is change notification fan-out, Observer is the right fit.
SOLID Alignment Observer supports SOLID principles clearly:
Open/Closed Principle Add new observers without modifying event producers.
Single Responsibility Principle Publisher emits events; each observer owns one downstream concern.
Dependency Inversion Principle Producer depends on observer abstractions, not concrete side-effect implementations.
This is why Observer is so effective for scaling side effects safely.
Common Mistakes 1. Hidden subscriber side effects If too much critical logic lives in observers, event flow becomes hard to trace. Keep ownership boundaries clear.
2. Unhandled observer failures Decide and document behavior: should one observer failure block others or not?
3. Missing idempotency For asynchronous or retried delivery paths, observer handlers should be idempotent.
4. Unbounded subscriber growth without observability Measure fan-out cost, latency, and failure rates. Event systems need explicit operational visibility.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Observer when:
one domain event has multiple independent reactions producer/consumer decoupling is valuable new side effects are expected over time Avoid Observer when:
there is only one tightly coupled reaction and no likely growth event propagation adds unnecessary indirection strict synchronous sequencing is mandatory and simpler direct orchestration is clearer Pattern value comes from decoupling real variation, not creating abstraction by default.
Final Thoughts The Observer pattern remains one of the most important patterns in modern software because event-driven behavior is everywhere.
In Java, Observer gives teams a clear way to separate core state changes from downstream reactions without hardcoding every side effect into one service.
Used well, it improves extensibility and keeps producer logic stable while subscribers evolve. Used carelessly, it creates hidden coupling and hard-to-debug event flow.
The practical standard is straightforward:
model meaningful domain events keep producer contracts clean isolate subscriber responsibilities design for failure handling and observability That is how you scale event-driven behavior without losing control of system complexity.

  • a payment succeeds, then receipts are sent
  • a user registers, then analytics and onboarding flows run

The State Pattern Solves a Workflow Complexity Problem Many systems have entities whose behavior depends on lifecycle stage:
orders move from created to paid to shipped accounts move from active to suspended to closed documents move from draft to approved to archived jobs move from queued to running to completed/failed The common failure mode is to keep lifecycle logic in one class with large conditional branches:
if (status == CREATED) { ... } else if (status == PAID) { ... } else if (status == SHIPPED) { ... } As transitions and rules grow, that central class becomes fragile and hard to reason about.
The State pattern solves this by representing each state as an object and delegating behavior to the current state. State transitions become explicit, and behavior changes with state without giant conditionals.
In Java systems, this is one of the cleanest ways to model lifecycle-driven behavior.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines State as:
Allow an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes. The object will appear to change its class.
In practical terms:
define a state interface for state-dependent behavior implement concrete states with transition rules keep a context object that holds current state delegate behavior calls from context to current state This keeps transition behavior localized and easier to evolve.
Why Teams Use State Without State, lifecycle logic often becomes:
one large method with nested branching duplicated transition checks across services inconsistent rule enforcement between call paths difficult unit tests for edge transitions With State:
each state owns behavior for that stage legal transitions are explicit invalid transitions fail clearly tests can target state-by-state rules directly This is especially useful in transactional workflows and domain-rich services.
Java Example: Order Lifecycle State interface public interface OrderState { void pay(OrderContext context); void ship(OrderContext context); void cancel(OrderContext context); String name(); } Context public class OrderContext { private OrderState state; private final String orderId; public OrderContext(String orderId) { this.orderId = orderId; this.state = new CreatedState(); } public String orderId() { return orderId; } public String currentState() { return state.name(); } void transitionTo(OrderState newState) { this.state = newState; } public void pay() { state.pay(this); } public void ship() { state.ship(this); } public void cancel() { state.cancel(this); } } Concrete states public class CreatedState implements OrderState { @Override public void pay(OrderContext context) { context.transitionTo(new PaidState()); } @Override public void ship(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot ship an order that has not been paid"); } @Override public void cancel(OrderContext context) { context.transitionTo(new CancelledState()); } @Override public String name() { return "CREATED"; } } public class PaidState implements OrderState { @Override public void pay(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Order is already paid"); } @Override public void ship(OrderContext context) { context.transitionTo(new ShippedState()); } @Override public void cancel(OrderContext context) { context.transitionTo(new CancelledState()); } @Override public String name() { return "PAID"; } } public class ShippedState implements OrderState { @Override public void pay(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot pay a shipped order"); } @Override public void ship(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Order is already shipped"); } @Override public void cancel(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot cancel a shipped order"); } @Override public String name() { return "SHIPPED"; } } public class CancelledState implements OrderState { @Override public void pay(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot pay a cancelled order"); } @Override public void ship(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot ship a cancelled order"); } @Override public void cancel(OrderContext context) { throw new IllegalStateException("Order is already cancelled"); } @Override public String name() { return "CANCELLED"; } } Usage OrderContext order = new OrderContext("ord-1001"); System.out.println(order.currentState()); // CREATED order.pay(); System.out.println(order.currentState()); // PAID order.ship(); System.out.println(order.currentState()); // SHIPPED This gives explicit transition behavior without central branching logic.
Another Java Example: Document Publishing State also helps with approval workflows:
DraftState InReviewState PublishedState ArchivedState Each state can enforce allowed actions:
only draft can submit for review only reviewed can publish only published can archive This avoids policy drift across controllers/services because transition rules live in one model.
State vs Strategy These patterns look similar structurally but differ in intent:
Strategy selects an interchangeable algorithm. State changes behavior as lifecycle state transitions over time. If behavior choice is based on configuration or policy, Strategy is often right.
If behavior evolves as an entity progresses through a lifecycle, State is usually right.
State vs Finite State Machine Libraries For small to moderate workflows, classic State objects are often enough.
For highly complex workflows with dozens of transitions, guard conditions, and side effects, a dedicated state machine library may be a better operational fit.
The pattern still applies conceptually; libraries simply formalize and instrument it.
SOLID Alignment State naturally supports SOLID principles:
Single Responsibility Principle Each state class owns behavior and transition rules for one lifecycle stage.
Open/Closed Principle You can add new states or transition rules with minimal impact to existing states.
Dependency Inversion Principle Context depends on the OrderState abstraction, not concrete state internals.
This leads to cleaner lifecycle modeling and safer changes over time.
Common Mistakes 1. Transition logic split between context and states Keep transition rules in one place (usually state classes) to avoid contradictory behavior.
2. Silent invalid transitions Invalid transitions should fail explicitly with useful error messages.
3. Too much shared mutable data in states State objects should generally be stateless policy carriers; keep mutable entity data in context/domain model.
4. Excessive object churn without need For high-throughput paths, consider reusing immutable singleton state instances instead of allocating new ones each transition.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use State when:
lifecycle stages are real and behavior differs by stage transition rules are becoming complex branch-heavy status logic is spread across services Avoid State when:
there are only one or two states with trivial behavior differences simple enums and straightforward checks are clearer lifecycle behavior is unlikely to evolve Pattern discipline means matching abstraction level to real workflow complexity.
Final Thoughts The State pattern is one of the most useful behavioral patterns for systems where correctness depends on lifecycle rules.
In Java, it replaces brittle status conditionals with explicit state-specific behavior and transition boundaries.
Used well, State improves clarity, testability, and evolution of workflow-rich domains. Used carelessly, it can create unnecessary class proliferation for simple scenarios.
The practical standard is clear:
model meaningful states explicitly enforce transitions in one place fail invalid transitions loudly test each state’s legal and illegal actions That is how you keep lifecycle logic understandable as systems scale.
summary:
The State Pattern Solves a Workflow Complexity Problem

Many systems have entities whose behavior depends on lifecycle stage:

  • orders move from created to paid to shipped
  • accounts move from active to suspended to closed
  • documents move from draft to approved to archived
  • jobs move from queued to running to completed/failed

The common failure mode is to keep lifecycle logic in one class with large conditional branches:

  • if (status == CREATED) { ... }
  • else if (status == PAID) { ... }
  • else if (status == SHIPPED) { ... }

As transitions and rules grow, that central class becomes fragile and hard to reason about.
title: Design Patterns: State Pattern - Modeling Behavior Through Explicit State Transitions

content:
The Strategy Pattern Solves a Behavior Variation Problem Many systems start with one algorithm. Then product requirements split:
pricing rules vary by customer tier retry policy varies by endpoint sorting logic varies by context shipping logic varies by region and SLA The common anti-pattern is a growing if/else or switch chain embedded in one class.
That design works briefly, then becomes fragile. Every new variation requires editing existing logic, retesting broad paths, and managing side effects from unrelated branches.
The Strategy pattern solves this by encapsulating each algorithm in its own class behind a shared interface. The client chooses which strategy to use at runtime without changing the client’s core flow.
In Java systems, this is one of the most practical patterns for keeping behavior extensible and testable.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Strategy as:
Define a family of algorithms, encapsulate each one, and make them interchangeable. Strategy lets the algorithm vary independently from clients that use it.
Practically, this means:
define a strategy interface implement concrete strategy classes inject or select strategy in context/client code avoid hardcoded conditional branching in the client This makes behavior extension additive instead of invasive.
Why Teams Use Strategy Without Strategy, algorithm changes tend to create:
branching-heavy service methods duplicated pre/post processing logic tight coupling between decision logic and execution logic difficult unit testing of individual behavior variants With Strategy, each algorithm becomes a composable unit.
That improves:
readability change isolation test focus long-term maintainability Java Example: Shipping Cost Calculation Strategy interface public interface ShippingStrategy { long calculateCents(Order order); } Concrete strategies public class StandardShippingStrategy implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public long calculateCents(Order order) { return 799L; } } public class ExpressShippingStrategy implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public long calculateCents(Order order) { return 1999L; } } public class FreeShippingOverThresholdStrategy implements ShippingStrategy { private final long thresholdCents; public FreeShippingOverThresholdStrategy(long thresholdCents) { this.thresholdCents = thresholdCents; } @Override public long calculateCents(Order order) { return order.subtotalCents() >= thresholdCents ? 0L : 999L; } } Context public class CheckoutService { private final ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy; public CheckoutService(ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy) { this.shippingStrategy = shippingStrategy; } public long totalCents(Order order) { return order.subtotalCents() + shippingStrategy.calculateCents(order); } } public record Order(String id, long subtotalCents) {} Usage Order order = new Order("ord-123", 12_500L); CheckoutService checkout = new CheckoutService(new FreeShippingOverThresholdStrategy(10_000L)); long total = checkout.totalCents(order); System.out.println("Total cents: " + total); No branching in CheckoutService, and new shipping behavior can be added without modifying that class.
Another Java Example: Payment Retry Policy Retry behavior often varies by integration reliability profile.
Strategy public interface RetryStrategy { boolean shouldRetry(int attemptNumber, int statusCode); } Concrete strategies public class AggressiveRetryStrategy implements RetryStrategy { @Override public boolean shouldRetry(int attemptNumber, int statusCode) { return attemptNumber < 5 && statusCode >= 500; } } public class ConservativeRetryStrategy implements RetryStrategy { @Override public boolean shouldRetry(int attemptNumber, int statusCode) { return attemptNumber < 2 && statusCode == 503; } } Context public class PaymentClient { private final RetryStrategy retryStrategy; public PaymentClient(RetryStrategy retryStrategy) { this.retryStrategy = retryStrategy; } public void charge(String customerId, long amountCents) { int attempt = 0; int statusCode; do { attempt++; statusCode = simulateRemoteCall(customerId, amountCents, attempt); if (statusCode == 200) { return; } } while (retryStrategy.shouldRetry(attempt, statusCode)); throw new IllegalStateException("Charge failed with status " + statusCode); } private int simulateRemoteCall(String customerId, long amountCents, int attempt) { return attempt < 2 ? 503 : 200; } } The client workflow remains stable while retry policy changes independently.
Strategy vs State These patterns look similar structurally but differ in intent:
Strategy selects among interchangeable algorithms. State changes behavior based on internal state transitions over time. If behavior choice is configuration/policy-driven, Strategy is usually the fit.
If behavior evolves because object state transitions, State is often more appropriate.
Strategy vs Template Method Strategy uses composition and interchangeable objects. Template Method uses inheritance and fixed algorithm skeletons with overridable steps. In Java enterprise systems, Strategy is often preferred when runtime flexibility and testability are priorities.
SOLID Alignment Strategy is a direct expression of SOLID principles:
Open/Closed Principle New behaviors are added via new strategy classes, not by editing existing context logic.
Single Responsibility Principle Each strategy class owns one algorithmic concern.
Dependency Inversion Principle Context classes depend on abstractions (ShippingStrategy, RetryStrategy), not concrete algorithms.
This is why Strategy scales well as product logic evolves.
Common Mistakes 1. Too many trivial strategies Do not create class-per-line abstractions for minor differences that do not justify indirection.
2. Leaking context internals into strategies Keep strategy inputs focused and stable. Passing entire service internals increases coupling.
3. Strategy selection logic spread across the system Centralize selection at composition boundaries (configuration, factory, DI container) where possible.
4. Ignoring defaults Define safe default behavior. Missing strategy configuration should fail clearly or use an intentional baseline.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Strategy when:
algorithm variants are real and expected to grow you need runtime behavior selection testability of each algorithm matters branch-heavy logic is growing in a core service Avoid Strategy when:
there is one stable algorithm with low change likelihood indirection adds more complexity than it removes a straightforward method parameter or comparator is enough Use the pattern to reduce complexity, not to decorate simple code.
Final Thoughts The Strategy pattern remains one of the most useful behavioral patterns because it turns algorithm variation from a maintenance risk into a composable design choice.
In Java, it helps teams replace brittle conditional logic with explicit, testable, and swappable behavior modules.
Used well, Strategy makes services easier to evolve and reason about. Used carelessly, it can create unnecessary class sprawl.
The practical standard is clear:
extract meaningful algorithm families keep strategy contracts narrow centralize strategy selection test each strategy as production-critical logic That is how you keep behavior flexible without letting complexity spread through core workflows.

The Strategy Pattern Solves a Behavior Variation Problem

Many systems start with one algorithm. Then product requirements split:

  • pricing rules vary by customer tier
  • retry policy varies by endpoint
  • sorting logic varies by context
  • shipping logic varies by region and SLA

The common anti-pattern is a growing if/else or switch chain embedded in one class.

That design works briefly, then becomes fragile. Every new variation requires editing existing logic, retesting broad paths, and managing side effects from unrelated branches.
title: Design Patterns: Strategy Pattern - Replacing Conditionals with Interchangeable Behavior

content:
The Composite Pattern Solves a Hierarchy Handling Problem Many business domains are hierarchical:
folders and files menus and menu items organizations and teams UI containers and widgets product bundles and single products The pain appears when client code must constantly ask:
“Is this a leaf or a container?” “Do I call one method for a single item and another for groups?” That conditional branching spreads quickly and makes hierarchy logic harder to maintain.
The Composite pattern solves this by letting clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly through a shared interface.
In Java systems, this is one of the cleanest patterns for recursive structures because it gives a single API surface for both leaf nodes and grouped nodes.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Composite as:
Compose objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects uniformly.
In practical terms:
define a component interface implement leaves (atomic elements) implement composites (containers of components) keep operations available through the same component contract This removes type-specific handling from callers and keeps tree logic inside the structure itself.
Why Teams Use Composite Without Composite, clients usually build nested loops and type checks all over the codebase.
That causes:
duplicated traversal logic fragile recursion spread across services hard-to-evolve APIs when hierarchy depth changes With Composite, callers use one abstraction and let the structure handle recursion.
This improves clarity, especially in systems where tree depth and node combinations change over time.
Java Example: File System Tree Component public interface FileSystemNode { String name(); long sizeInBytes(); void print(String indent); } Leaf public class FileNode implements FileSystemNode { private final String name; private final long sizeInBytes; public FileNode(String name, long sizeInBytes) { this.name = name; this.sizeInBytes = sizeInBytes; } @Override public String name() { return name; } @Override public long sizeInBytes() { return sizeInBytes; } @Override public void print(String indent) { System.out.println(indent + "- " + name + " (" + sizeInBytes + " bytes)"); } } Composite import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class DirectoryNode implements FileSystemNode { private final String name; private final List<FileSystemNode> children = new ArrayList<>(); public DirectoryNode(String name) { this.name = name; } public void add(FileSystemNode child) { children.add(child); } public void remove(FileSystemNode child) { children.remove(child); } @Override public String name() { return name; } @Override public long sizeInBytes() { long total = 0L; for (FileSystemNode child : children) { total += child.sizeInBytes(); } return total; } @Override public void print(String indent) { System.out.println(indent + "+ " + name + "/"); for (FileSystemNode child : children) { child.print(indent + " "); } } } Usage public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { DirectoryNode root = new DirectoryNode("root"); DirectoryNode reports = new DirectoryNode("reports"); DirectoryNode logs = new DirectoryNode("logs"); reports.add(new FileNode("q1.pdf", 120_000)); reports.add(new FileNode("q2.pdf", 110_000)); logs.add(new FileNode("app.log", 2_000_000)); root.add(reports); root.add(logs); root.add(new FileNode("readme.txt", 3_000)); root.print(""); System.out.println("Total size: " + root.sizeInBytes()); } } Client code treats directories and files through the same FileSystemNode interface.
Another Java Example: Cart Items and Bundles Composite is also useful for pricing trees where a line item can be either a product or a bundle of products.
Component public interface CartItem { String label(); long priceCents(); } Leaf public class ProductItem implements CartItem { private final String label; private final long priceCents; public ProductItem(String label, long priceCents) { this.label = label; this.priceCents = priceCents; } @Override public String label() { return label; } @Override public long priceCents() { return priceCents; } } Composite import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; public class BundleItem implements CartItem { private final String label; private final List<CartItem> children = new ArrayList<>(); public BundleItem(String label) { this.label = label; } public void add(CartItem item) { children.add(item); } @Override public String label() { return label; } @Override public long priceCents() { long total = 0L; for (CartItem child : children) { total += child.priceCents(); } return total; } } This provides a unified pricing contract regardless of whether the line is atomic or nested.
Transparent vs Safe Composite There are two common design choices:
Transparent composite: child-management methods (add/remove) exist on the component interface.
easier for callers but leaves may expose unsupported operations Safe composite: child-management methods exist only on composite classes.
stronger type safety slightly more awareness required by callers when mutating trees The examples above use a safe composite approach, which is often better in Java codebases that prioritize explicitness.
Composite vs Decorator vs Visitor Composite models tree structures and part-whole recursion. Decorator adds behavior layers around a component. Visitor separates algorithms from object structures (often over composites). If your core problem is “single object and group should be treated the same,” Composite is usually the right fit.
SOLID Alignment Composite aligns well with SOLID principles:
Open/Closed Principle You can introduce new leaf/composite node types without changing callers that target the component interface.
Single Responsibility Principle Each node type owns its own behavior (for example, how it computes size or price).
Dependency Inversion Principle Clients depend on FileSystemNode or CartItem abstractions, not concrete node classes.
This helps recursive models stay extensible and predictable.
Common Mistakes 1. Pushing mutation APIs onto all nodes without guardrails If leaves expose add/remove and callers misuse them, runtime failures become common.
2. Embedding traversal logic everywhere Traversal should live close to the component model or in dedicated operations, not repeated in every client.
3. Ignoring recursion depth and performance Large trees can create expensive recursive operations. Cache or optimize where needed.
4. Mixing unrelated responsibilities into node classes Keep nodes focused on structure and domain behavior, not transport, persistence, and UI concerns all at once.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Composite when:
your domain is naturally hierarchical clients need uniform handling for single and grouped entities recursive behavior is central to the model Avoid Composite when:
there is no meaningful hierarchy flat structures are sufficient recursive abstraction introduces unnecessary complexity The pattern should simplify client code, not shift complexity into hidden recursion.
Final Thoughts The Composite pattern is one of the most useful structural patterns for domain models built around trees and part-whole relationships.
In Java, it gives teams a clean way to represent nested structures while preserving a uniform API for leaves and composites.
Used well, Composite reduces conditional branching and centralizes recursion in the model itself. Used poorly, it can introduce confusing mutation semantics and hidden performance costs.
The practical standard is clear:
model the hierarchy explicitly expose consistent component contracts choose transparent vs safe composition intentionally validate recursion behavior with real-world depth and size That is how you make hierarchical systems easier to reason about and evolve.

The Composite Pattern Solves a Hierarchy Handling Problem

Many business domains are hierarchical:

  • folders and files
  • menus and menu items
  • organizations and teams
  • UI containers and widgets
  • product bundles and single products

The pain appears when client code must constantly ask:

  • “Is this a leaf or a container?”
  • “Do I call one method for a single item and another for groups?”

That conditional branching spreads quickly and makes hierarchy logic harder to maintain.
title: Design Patterns: Composite Pattern - Treating Trees and Leaves Uniformly

content:
The Proxy Pattern Solves an Access and Control Problem In real systems, not every object should be called directly.
Sometimes you need:
authorization checks lazy loading for expensive resources remote invocation boundaries request throttling caching and fallback behavior The core object should still do its job, but callers may need controlled access to it.
That is where the Proxy pattern fits.
Proxy provides a substitute or placeholder for another object to control access to it. In Java systems, it is a practical way to insert operational policy around a component while keeping the component’s core logic unchanged.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four defines Proxy as:
Provide a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it.
In practical terms:
the proxy implements the same interface as the real subject callers interact with the proxy as if it were the real object the proxy decides how and when to delegate The pattern is most useful when control concerns are real and repeated.
Why Teams Use Proxy in Production Without a proxy, control logic often leaks into business code:
auth checks repeated in multiple services ad hoc remote retry/circuit logic spread across clients lazy initialization logic duplicated per call site A proxy centralizes those policies.
It lets you keep business interfaces stable while enforcing operational rules in one place.
Java Example: Protection Proxy for Authorization Subject interface public interface DocumentService { String read(String documentId, UserContext userContext); } Real subject public class RealDocumentService implements DocumentService { @Override public String read(String documentId, UserContext userContext) { return "Document content for " + documentId; } } Proxy public class AuthorizationDocumentProxy implements DocumentService { private final DocumentService delegate; public AuthorizationDocumentProxy(DocumentService delegate) { this.delegate = delegate; } @Override public String read(String documentId, UserContext userContext) { if (!userContext.hasRole("DOCUMENT_READ")) { throw new SecurityException("User is not authorized to read documents"); } return delegate.read(documentId, userContext); } } public record UserContext(String userId, java.util.Set<String> roles) { public boolean hasRole(String role) { return roles.contains(role); } } This keeps authorization at the boundary and domain behavior in the real service.
Java Example: Virtual Proxy for Lazy Loading A virtual proxy is useful when object initialization is expensive.
Subject interface public interface ReportRenderer { String render(); } Expensive real subject public class HeavyReportRenderer implements ReportRenderer { public HeavyReportRenderer() { // simulate expensive startup try { Thread.sleep(1000); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); throw new IllegalStateException("Initialization interrupted", e); } } @Override public String render() { return "Rendered high-fidelity report"; } } Lazy proxy public class LazyReportRendererProxy implements ReportRenderer { private volatile ReportRenderer delegate; @Override public String render() { if (delegate == null) { synchronized (this) { if (delegate == null) { delegate = new HeavyReportRenderer(); } } } return delegate.render(); } } This defers expensive initialization until the first real call.
Java Example: Remote Proxy Boundary A remote proxy makes local code look like a local call while delegating over the network.
public interface CustomerProfileClient { CustomerProfile getProfile(String customerId); } public class HttpCustomerProfileClientProxy implements CustomerProfileClient { private final HttpGateway gateway; public HttpCustomerProfileClientProxy(HttpGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; } @Override public CustomerProfile getProfile(String customerId) { String path = "/customers/" + customerId; String json = gateway.get(path); return CustomerProfile.fromJson(json); } } public record CustomerProfile(String customerId, String email) { public static CustomerProfile fromJson(String json) { // simplified parsing for example purposes return new CustomerProfile("customer-123", "user@example.com"); } } This isolates transport and serialization concerns from business services.
Common Proxy Variants In practice, you will see these proxy types frequently:
Protection proxy: enforces authorization/policy Virtual proxy: lazy-loads expensive objects Remote proxy: represents remote services locally Caching proxy: caches results before delegating Logging/monitoring proxy: captures telemetry around calls These are all the same structural idea: same interface, controlled delegation.
Proxy vs Decorator vs Adapter These patterns are similar structurally but different in intent:
Proxy controls access to an object. Decorator adds behavior/responsibilities compositionally. Adapter translates incompatible interfaces. If your concern is access control, lifecycle, remoting, or policy gates, Proxy is usually the right fit.
SOLID Alignment Proxy can reinforce SOLID principles when applied deliberately:
Single Responsibility Principle Control concerns (auth, caching, remoting) live in proxies; domain logic remains in real subjects.
Open/Closed Principle You can add new proxy behaviors without modifying existing subject implementations.
Dependency Inversion Principle Clients depend on stable interfaces, not concrete classes or transport details.
This is why Proxy scales well in layered Java architectures.
Common Mistakes 1. Putting domain logic in the proxy Proxy should govern access and delegation, not become the business service.
2. Hiding expensive side effects If a proxy adds network calls or retries, document it. “Looks local” can mislead performance expectations.
3. Building deep proxy chains without observability Multiple wrappers can obscure behavior. Use clear naming and telemetry.
4. Weak error semantics Proxies should normalize errors thoughtfully, not swallow failure details that operators need.
Practical Guidance for Java Teams Use Proxy when:
you need policy enforcement at call boundaries object creation should be deferred remote integration details should stay isolated cross-cutting control concerns need consistency Avoid Proxy when:
direct invocation is already simple and safe added indirection provides no operational value proxy layers make debugging harder than the control benefit they provide Pattern discipline means using proxy for real control concerns, not cosmetic abstraction.
Final Thoughts The Proxy pattern is one of the most practical patterns in enterprise Java because it handles a common reality: access to behavior often needs governance.
Used well, Proxy keeps interfaces stable while enforcing authorization, lazy loading, remote boundaries, and operational policy in one place. Used poorly, it hides complexity and obscures performance characteristics.
The right approach is straightforward:
keep proxy intent explicit keep subject interfaces clean separate control concerns from domain concerns test policy and delegation paths as production-critical behavior That is how you add control without contaminating core business logic.
